intent: Eight individual questions distinguish doer, recipient, possession, thing, bounded comparison, location, cause and method without inventing unknown answers.
picturePurpose: Original refill scene supplies a fictional location contrast. Exact path steps and swap-dependent selection are coded; no real water-safety or opening claim.

transfer.stem: Which note correctly identifies the information requested?
transfer.passage:
Questions before the club walk
Our club checked the questions for a walking-trip worksheet. “Who left these boots by the door?” asked for the person who left them, not necessarily their owner. “To whom should I send the completed form?” asked for the recipient; the speaker was the sender. “Whose name is missing from the list?” asked about a name, and a missing name did not prove that a person was absent.
A model-building question asked what kept two pieces together. It did not give the answer, so we could not simply assume it was glue. The route question asked which path had fewer steps. A path with fewer steps was not necessarily shorter in distance.
A fictional park picture showed a bottle receiving water from a blue refill fixture on the left. The picnic table and backpack were on the right. The picture illustrated a place answer, not proof of water safety or real opening hours.
Finally, “Why did the water change colour?” asked for a cause, whereas “How did you make the corners so neat?” asked for a method. Neither question supplied its own answer. We decided to identify the information being requested before trying to answer it.

options.text: To whom asks for the recipient; fewer steps compares step counts; why asks for a cause and how asks for a method.
To whom asks for the sender; fewer steps compares step counts; why asks for a cause and how asks for a method.
To whom asks for the recipient; fewer steps proves a shorter distance; why asks for a cause and how asks for a method.
